statements.claim: Guards in Shonitapura discover an unknown young man in the king's inner apartments and report it to the king.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.26-28: the guards report to the king that his daughter has been enjoyed by a Yadava hero ('yadu-vīreṇa bhujyamānāṃ hata-vratām'); VP 5.33: 'The guards of the inner apartments discovering him there with Ushá, reported it to the king.'

statements.claim: Usha is the daughter of Bana, king of Shonitapura, and Aniruddha is the son of Pradyumna and grandson of Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.27-30 ('duhituḥ... kāmātmajam'), index entry and corpus chain; HV 1.266 identifies 'Pradyumna's son' Aniruddha and Usha as Vāna's daughter.

statements.claim: Usha had dreamed of a handsome young prince and fallen in love with the dream; the goddess's boon promised she would marry the man she saw.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266 (in pack): Usha chose Aniruddha 'on account of the boon given by the goddess', and Chitralekha tells him 'Ushā whom you saw in a dream and married'; background beat of DKS_0342 (corpus chain).

statements.claim: Her friend Chitralekha, skilled in the arts of illusion, brought Aniruddha from Dwaraka to Usha, and the two were united in the palace.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266: Chitralekha uses Tamasik illusion to carry Aniruddha to Shonitapura; VP 5.33: 'a female, possessed of magic faculties, conveyed him'; BP 10.62.26 confirms the secret union.

statements.claim: Bana, son of Bali, rushes in fury to the women's quarters and finds his daughter at dice with Aniruddha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.29-31: 'tataḥ pravyathito bāṇo duhituḥ śruta-dūṣaṇaḥ... dīvyantam akṣaiḥ' — Bana, agitated at his daughter's defilement, sees him dicing with her; HV/VP agree.

statements.claim: Aniruddha is described as beautiful beyond compare, dark as a rain cloud, lotus-eyed, saffron-clad, with Usha's red kumkuma on his chest where she had leaned.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.30-31: 'bhuvanaika-sundaraṃ śyāmaṃ piśaṅgāmbaram ambujekṣaṇam... tad-aṅga-saṅga-stana-kuṅkuma-srajam' — world's one beauty, dark, saffron-clad, lotus-eyed, kumkuma from her breasts' contact on his body.

statements.claim: Aniruddha scatters the guards like a great boar scattering dogs, whereupon Bana binds him with serpent-nooses so he cannot move.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.33-34: he strikes the guards creeping like dogs 'śūkara-yūthapaḥ' (like a boar-leader) and 'taṃ nāga-pāśair... babandha ha' (bound him with serpent-nooses); HV: chained with serpents; VP: serpent bonds. The story's living-serpent framing follows BP (its own tradition_note flags the HV serpentine-shafts variant).

statements.claim: Kumbhanda counsels that the prince should not be slain; Aniruddha is handed over to the guards and kept bound, and Bana withdraws to his own apartments.
statements.evidence: HV 1.266: Kumbhānda said 'He does not deserve to be slain', Aniruddha is 'handing over... to the guards', and Vāna 'repaired to his own palace'; VP 5.33: Bana (having tried to kill the prince) 'followed the counsel of his minister' and captured him by magic.

statements.claim: The hidden union will bring war: someone in Dwaraka will count the children of the house of Yadu and find one missing.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing bridge; Narada's report to the Yadavas and the count of the missing prince belong to the next episode (BP 10.63.1, DKS_0344), not asserted in this pack.

notes: Faithful to BP 10.62.26-34 with HV 1.266/VP 5.33 support. The 'thrown into a cell' locale is the corpus's own framing (also DKS_0346/0347) — no pack source places him in a cell, and HV 1.276 has him remain bound in the women's apartment until release; judged a narrative setting choice, not a sourced fact error.

statements.claim: Narada tells the Yadavas that Aniruddha has been taken and is Bana's prisoner in Shonitapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.1: 'nāradāt tad upākarṇya vārtāṃ baddhasya karma ca' (hearing from Narada the news of the bound one); VP 5.33: 'Nárada came to them, and told them that he was the prisoner of Báńa... in Śońitapura.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Satyaki, Gada and Samba, with twelve full armies, besiege Shonitapura, breaking its parks, ramparts, towers and gateways.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.2-4: 'pradyumno yuyudhānaś ca gadaḥ sāmbo... akṣauhiṇībhir dvādaśabhiḥ... bhajyamāna-purodyāna-prākārāṭṭāla-gopuram' — twelve akṣauhiṇīs; parks, ramparts, towers (aṭṭāla) and gateways (gopura) being broken.

statements.claim: Bana is a devotee of Shiva, and for his sake Shiva takes the field with his son Skanda beside him and his strange hosts around him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.5: 'bāṇārthe bhagavān rudraḥ sa-sutaḥ pramathair vṛtaḥ' (Rudra with his son, surrounded by pramathas, for Bana's sake); HV 1.272: Kumāra (Skanda) also mounts a car; the attendant hosts (bhūta, pramatha, guhyaka) appear in BP 10.63.9-10.

statements.claim: The battle was dreadful, hair-raising and wonderful beyond mortal experience.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.6: 'āsīt su-tumulaṃ yuddham adbhutaṃ roma-harṣaṇam' — exceedingly tumultuous, wonderful, hair-raising.

statements.claim: The demon commanders Kumbhanda and Kupakarna hurl themselves at Balarama.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.7: 'kumbhāṇḍa-kūpakarṇābhyāṃ balena saha saṃyugaḥ' (engagement of Kumbhanda and Kupakarna with Bala[rama]); they later fall struck by the muṣala, Balarama's weapon (BP 10.63.15 in DKS_0345 pack).

statements.claim: Riding Garuda, Krishna and the Yadava heroes disperse the Danava army with arrow-fire; the Danavas flee despite Bana's rallying cry ('born in the race of the Daityas'), and only the pramathas hold their ground.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: the three heroes on Garuda disperse the Dānava army with a downpour of arrows; fire from Krishna's arrows consumes thousands of Dānavas; Vāna shouts 'Born in the race of the Daityas why do ye... fly away?'; the Dānavas flee nonetheless and 'only the Pramathas stood firm'.

statements.claim: Shiva, eyes reddened with anger to protect Bana, mounts his great car drawn by lions and ringed by howling ghosts — with faces of tigers, serpents and horses, blowing conches, some in bark with matted locks — a car that seemed to devour the sky.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: 'Siva... had his eyes reddened with anger. And in order to protect Vāna, he stood on his lustrous car... drawn by lions... as if devouring the sky'; the ghost-train with faces of tigers/serpents/horses, blowing conch-shells, some 'put on bark', some with 'matted locks', is described in the same passage.

statements.claim: Shiva looses the Brahma, wind, fire and Pashupata weapons; Krishna answers each with a match — Brahma answered by Brahma, the wind-weapon by the mountain-weapon — then Vishnu's Indra-given weapon flies at Rudra's car, Shiva's fiery weapon covers the heroes, the Varuna weapon quenches the fire, and the Vaishnava weapon routs the bhutas, yakshas and asuras.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.11-12 + pack summary: 'Krishna countered Shiva's Brahma, wind, fire and Pashupata weapons with matching astras' (brahmāstrasya brahmāstram, vāyavyasya pārvatam); HV 1.272: 'Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra... Hara discharged the highly dreadful fiery weapon... Vāsudeva took up Vāruna weapon... fire... extinguished... Mādhava discharged his Vaishnava weapon... all the Bhutas, Yakshas and Asuras... fled on all sides.'

statements.claim: Brahma himself came with the celestials, and Apsaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Charanas crowded the sky to watch, while the earth was scorched, the mountains shaken and the quarters ablaze.
statements.evidence: HV 1.272: the Grandfather (Brahmā) came encircled by the celestials; Apsaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Chāranas witnessed the encounter; 'the quarters, sky and earth were as if all ablaze', mountains were covered with streams and their summits scattered.

statements.claim: Neither Shiva nor Krishna had yielded, and the duel would end only by a yawn.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing bridge to DKS_0345; the pack's verses end with the weapons still exchanged (BP 10.63.1-12; HV 1.272 breaks off mid-passage), and the Jrimbhana-astra resolution belongs to BP 10.63.13.

notes: Combines BP 10.63.1-12 and HV 1.272 as the pack itself does; both agree on the core weapon-exchange sequence. HV's 'Krishna and the three other heroes were covered with arrows' vs the story's 'three Yadava heroes' is negligible compression.

statements.claim: Krishna looses the Jrimbhana weapon, the astra of yawning, and strikes Shiva in the midst of his wrath; the god gapes uncontrollably, sinks down in his car and can no longer fight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.13: 'mohayitvā tu giriśaṃ jṛmbhaṇāstreṇa jṛmbhitam' (stupefying Girisha, made him yawn with the Jrimbhana astra); VP 5.33: 'Hara, overcome with incessant gaping, sat down in his car, and was unable longer to contend with Krishńa.'

statements.claim: Krishna's army falls on Bana's host and breaks it utterly.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered BP excerpt (10.63.13-20): 'Krishna, stupefying Shiva with the Jrimbhana weapon, slew Bana's army'.

statements.claim: Skanda tries to hold his father's cause together but, bloodied under Pradyumna's arrows from every side, takes to flight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.14: 'skandaḥ pradyumna-bāṇaughair ardyamānaḥ samantataḥ' (Skanda tormented on all sides by Pradyumna's arrow-floods); VP 5.33: 'Kártikeya, wounded... took to flight.'

statements.claim: Kumbhanda and Kupakarna, the demon commanders, are struck down and fall.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.15: 'kumbhāṇḍa-kūpakarṇaś ca petatur muṣalārditau' (Kumbhanda and Kupakarna fell, struck by the muṣala).

statements.claim: Seeing his army shattered, Bana in fury seizes five hundred bows at once and shoots at Krishna; the discus in Krishna's hand cuts all five hundred bows down together.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.16-18: 'viśīryamāṇam sva-balaṃ dṛṣṭvā bāṇo 'ty-amarṣitaḥ / dhanūṃṣy ākṛṣya yugapad bāṇaḥ pañca-śatāni vai / tāni ciccheda bhagavān dhanūṃsi yugapad dhariḥ' — Bana drew five hundred bows at once and Hari cut them all simultaneously.

statements.claim: Kotara, Bana's mother, comes onto the field and stands before the conqueror with her hair unbound and without a veil, offering her own dignity so her son may live.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.19: 'tan-mātā koṭarā nāma nagnā makta-śiroruhā' — his mother Kotara, naked, with hair unbound; pack summary: she 'stood naked before Krishna to save her son's life'. The story's 'hair unbound and without a veil' is a modest rendering of nagnā (naked); same gesture, deliberate softening, not a substantive divergence.

statements.claim: Krishna turns his face aside and will not look upon her; the lingering ghostly hosts take the sign and flee, and the slaughter stops.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.20-21: 'tatas tiryaṅ-mukho nagnām anirīkṣan gadāgrajaḥ' (face averted, not looking at the naked one) and 'vidrāvite bhūta-gaṇe' (the host of bhūtas scattered).

statements.claim: Bana himself still stands, his thousand arms still his own; the discus has not yet done its work.
statements.evidence: Bridge to DKS_0346: in the BP sequence the arm-cutting (10.63.30-48) follows the Kotara/Fever episodes (10.63.19-29), so the line is chronologically consistent but is narrative scene-setting rather than a sourced event in this pack's verses.

notes: Ordering matches BP 10.63.13-20 exactly (Jrimbhana, Skanda, Kumbhanda/Kupakarna, five hundred bows, Kotara). Only handling of note: BP's 'naked' rendered as 'hair unbound and without a veil' — an age-appropriate softening flagged above, kept as SUPPORTED since the act (unveiling/self-exposure to shield her son) is intact.

statements.claim: Bana boasts to Krishna: 'You will not escape me alive today. I have a thousand arms, and you have eight — how will you fight me? You will see my thousand arms multiply into a million.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'Wait! Wait! You will not escape from me to-day alive... being of eight arms how you will be able to fight with me who have a thousand arms?... You will see to-day my thousand arms... multiply into a million.'

statements.claim: Narada, watching from the palace roof, laughs aloud until the sky seems to split.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'Hearing those proud words of Vāna Nārada so laughed aloud that as if the sky was sundered in twain'; later the same account places him 'sitting on the highest top of the palace'.

statements.claim: Krishna answers: 'Heroes do not vaunt. Come and fight.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'The heroes do not vaunt thus. What is the use of vaunting? Come and fight with me in the battle field.'

statements.claim: Bana covers Krishna with clubs, maces, spears and the rest, and when Krishna's arrows cut him to the quick he discharges the celestial astra that Brahma had long ago created for Hiranyakashipu.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: Vāna 'covered Keshava' with parighas, clubs, tomaras, śaktis, maces and pattiśas; then 'discharged that celestial great weapon... which Brahmā, by his ascetic powers, had formerly created for Hiranyakashipu.'

statements.claim: The weapon shrouds everything in darkness and rains burning arrows; Krishna's Indra-given weapon dispels the darkness, quenches the fire, the gods laugh like lions and the Danavas lose heart.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: 'all the quarters were enshrouded with darkness... A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused'; with Indra's weapon 'all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished and the Dānavas completely lost their hearts... the gods began to laugh and roar like lions.'

statements.claim: Arrows from Krishna's great bow Sharnga shatter Bana's car with horses and standards, strip away his crown, mail, bow and shield, and a winged arrow strikes him on the breast, so that he swoons.
statements.evidence: HV 1.275: from the Śārṅga bow Keshava 'sundered Vāna's car, with horses and standards, into pieces', 'separated... his... crown, coat of mail, bow and shield', 'struck him on the breast with winged arrows', and 'Vāna lost his consciousness and swooned away.'

statements.claim: Bana rises and rushes at Krishna with all his thousand arms bearing every weapon; the Sudarshana discus severs the arms one by one, like a man pruning branches, until his terrible strength is gone.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.30-31: 'tato bāhu-sahasreṇa nānāyudha-dharo 'suraḥ... cakreṇa kṣura-neminā' (the Asura with his thousand arms bearing various weapons; [Krishna] with the razor-edged discus); pack summary: arms 'cut off... as if pruning branches'; HV 1.275: the discus 'gradually cutting off Vāna's thousand arms'.

statements.claim: Shiva — recovered from the yawning weapon — watches his devotee's arms fall, hymns Krishna as the primal person, the single source of all worlds, the sun hidden only by its own light, and pleads: 'This one is dear to me. He has followed me; I have given him freedom from fear.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.32-44: Rudra speaks while Bana's arms are cut (10.63.32-33), praising 'tvam eka ādyaḥ puruṣo 'dvitīyas' and 'yathaiva sūryaḥ pihitaś chāyayā svayā'; v.44: 'ayaṃ mameṣṭo dayito 'nuvartī mayābhayaṃ dattam amuṣya deva' — near-verbatim match.

statements.claim: Krishna spares Bana in honor of the boon given long ago to Prahlada: 'This Asura is not to be killed, even by me. His arms were cut to humble his pride.' He leaves Bana four arms, freedom from fear, and ageless, deathless life.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.46-48: 'avadhyo 'yaṃ mamāpy eṣa vairocani-suto 'suraḥ / darpopaśamanāyāsya pravṛkṇā bāhavo mayā / catvāro 'sya bhujāḥ śiṣṭā bhaviṣyaty ajarāmaraḥ'; pack summary confirms the sparing honors 'the boon given to Prahrada'. Variant noted in pack: HV/VP leave two arms; the story follows BP's four (its primary source).

statements.claim: Bana, who had imagined a million arms, stands humbled with four; the war for Aniruddha is over and the prince's release is imminent.
statements.evidence: Closing tableau and bridge to DKS_0347; consistent with BP 10.63.48-49 (four arms remain; fearlessness granted) but phrased as narration rather than a sourced event in this pack.

notes: Blends HV 1.275 (boast, weapon-duel, swoon) with BP 10.63.20-48 (arm-cutting, Shiva's hymns, sparing) exactly as the pack presents both. Arms remaining: four per BP (primary) vs two per HV/VP — story correctly follows BP and the pack flags the variant.

statements.claim: Aniruddha had been carried off by magic to Shonitapura; Usha loved him, and Bana kept the young prince prisoner, bound with serpent-nooses, in the women's quarters.
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: Narada tells Krishna the prince 'is waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment'; the abduction-by-magic and serpent-bondage match BP 10.62/VP 5.33 (corpus chain: DKS_0343-0346).

statements.claim: Krishna's discus severed Bana's thousand arms one after another, until the demon king stood before his conqueror; yet Krishna spared him — at Shiva's plea, and because Bana, even in defeat, had bowed to him.
statements.evidence: Compressed recap of DKS_0346: the severing (BP 10.63.30-31) and sparing at Shiva's plea plus the Prahlada boon (BP 10.63.44-48) are supported, but two nuances are smoothed over: Bana was left four arms, not 'armless', and BP 10.63.49 has him bow his head only after receiving fearlessness — the bow did not motivate the mercy. The sentence is faithful in substance, loose in causal ordering; flagged as narration rather than error.

statements.claim: Krishna had pressed the sage Narada again and again for word of the boy: 'My mind is overpowered with affection... I wish to see even today Aniruddha, who has slain his enemies.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: 'O reverend sir, my mind is overpowered with affection... I wish to see even to-day Aniruddha who has his enemies slain.' Near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Granted fearlessness, Bana comes forward and touches his head to Krishna's feet.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.49: 'iti labdhvābhayaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ praṇamya śirasāsuraḥ' — obtaining fearlessness, the Asura bowed his head to Krishna.

statements.claim: Bana places Aniruddha and his bride Usha on a chariot, gives them an escort from his own army, and sends them home with the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: Pack's BP excerpt (10.63.49-52): 'Bana bowed to Krishna, placed Aniruddha and his bride Usha on a chariot, and sent them with an army'; BP 10.63.50 shows Aniruddha 'akṣauhiṇyā parivṛtaṃ su-vāsaḥ-samalaṅkṛtam' (surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī, well-dressed and adorned).

statements.claim: During Aniruddha's absence Dwaraka had been full of anxious talk, a son of the house spirited away with no one certain whether he lived.
statements.evidence: HV 1.276: 'The heroic Aniruddha being taken away stealthily the city of Dwārakā is filled with anxiety.'

statements.claim: Word runs ahead of the returning host and Dwaraka prepares as for a festival: banners on the walls, arches raised at the crossings, streets and squares swept and sprinkled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.51: the capital is adorned 'dhvajaiḥ sa-toraṇair ukṣita-mārga-catvarām' — with flags, with arches, its streets and squares sprinkled; the story's 'swept and sprinkled' matches ukṣita.

statements.claim: Krishna enters his own capital to the blare of conches and roll of drums, greeted by citizens, friends and priests.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.51: 'viveśa śaṅkhānaka-dundubhi-svanair abhyudyataḥ paura-suhṛd-dvijātibhiḥ' — entered amid the sound of conches and dundubhi drums, welcomed by citizens, friends and brahmins.

statements.claim: At the heart of the procession ride Aniruddha with Usha beside him — the prince the city had feared lost and the bride who came back with him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.63.50 (Aniruddha returning adorned and escorted) and the pack summary placing the couple on a chariot sent with the army; the couple's return to Dwaraka is the episode's point. (Variant: HV 1.276 has Usha ride on a peacock with a goddess while the four heroes sit on Garuda; the story follows the BP reading.)

statements.claim: Long after the procession passed, the sound of the conches carried out over the water, telling the sea the house of Yadu had its prince back.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric closing image; Dwaraka is a coastal city in the corpus, but the detail is rhetorical, not a sourced fact.

notes: One deliberate caution: the recap glosses the order of Bana's mercy (bow vs. four arms remaining) — see the RCN statement. Otherwise BP 10.63.49-52 and HV 1.276 both support the surrender, escort and triumphal return.

statements.claim: Shalva's army appears everywhere and nowhere at once — on the ground, in the sky, on mountain peaks, in the water — now a single host, now many, one form and many forms, seen and unseen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.20-22: 'bahu-rūpaika-rūpaṃ tad dṛśyate na ca dṛśyate / kvacid bhūmau kvacid vyomni giri-mūrdhni jale kvacit' — many-formed and one-formed, seen and not seen, now on earth, now in the sky, on mountain tops, sometimes in water.

statements.claim: Shalva, an old enemy of the house of Yadu, had come against Dwaraka again with sorcery and numbers.
statements.evidence: Contextual framing: the pack places the engagement at Dwaraka (index location) within the ongoing Shalva war (BP 10.76), and Shalva's earlier enmity with the Yadus is established in earlier episodes of the corpus; the excerpt itself, however, begins mid-engagement and does not recount the siege or prior enmity.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Krishna's son, rides out to meet him and in a single moment dispels the demon's illusions with his divine weapons, reading the false shapes in the air.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.76.17-32): 'Pradyumna in a moment dispels the demon's illusions with divine weapons'; the illusory many-form/one-form army of vv.20-22 is what he reads through.

statements.claim: Pradyumna drives twenty-five iron-headed arrows with golden shafts into Shalva himself, strikes the king with a hundred more, and then fells his soldiers one arrow apiece.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.17-18: 'vivyādha pañca-viṃśatyā svarṇa-puṅkhair ayo-mukhaiḥ / śatenātāḍayac chālvam ekaikenāsya sainikān' — pierced [Shalva] with twenty-five gold-shafted, iron-tipped arrows; struck Shalva with a hundred; each soldier with one.

statements.claim: It was a wonderful deed, and warriors of both armies stopped to watch.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.19: 'tad adbhutaṃ mahat karma pradyumnasya mahātmanaḥ' (that wonderful great deed of the great-souled Pradyumna); pack summary: 'winning the admiration of both armies'.

statements.claim: Shalva's arrows — hot as fire and sun, unapproachable as serpent poison — fall in floods on the Vrishni heroes, and Pradyumna's own side is hard pressed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.23-24: 'śarair agny-arka-saṃsparśair āśī-viṣa-durāsadaiḥ... vṛṣṇi-vīrā bhṛśārditāḥ' — with arrows of fire-sun touch, unapproachable like snake-venom, the Vrishni heroes were greatly afflicted.

statements.claim: Dyuman, Shalva's minister — himself wounded and pressed hard by Pradyumna earlier — seizes a mace and strikes the young warrior full on the chest; his armor gives way and the charioteer carries the senseless hero from the field.
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.25-27: 'śālvāmātyo dyumān nāma pradyumnaṃ prak prapīḍitaḥ / pradyumnaṃ gadayā sīrṇa-vakṣaḥ-sthalam' — Dyuman, earlier oppressed by Pradyumna, shattered his chest with a mace; pack summary confirms the charioteer 'carries the senseless hero away'.

statements.claim: Regaining consciousness, Pradyumna rebukes his charioteer: 'No one born in the line of the Yadus is ever heard of as one who fled the field. What shall I say when I come before my two fathers, Rama and Keshava? My brothers' wives will laugh when they tell of this.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.27-30: 'labdha-samjño muhūrtena kārṣṇiḥ sārathim abravīt / na yadūnāṃ kule jātaḥ śrūyate raṇa-vicyutaḥ / kiṃ nu vakṣye 'bhisaṅgamya pitarau rāma-keśavau / vyaktaṃ me kathayiṣyanti hasantyo bhrātṛ-jāmayaḥ' — near-verbatim, including 'both fathers Rāma and Keśava'.

statements.claim: The charioteer answers: 'Knowing this, I carried you from the battle.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.76.31-32: 'sārathir uvāca / etad viditvā tu bhavān mayāpovāhito raṇāt' — 'Knowing this, you were carried away by me from the battle.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, steadying himself on the rail of the chariot, looks back toward the battle.
statements.evidence: Closing tableau continuing from BP 10.76.27 (he recovers and speaks in the chariot); the specific posture is scene-setting, not a sourced event.

notes: Very tight to BP 10.76.17-32; numbers, names (Dyuman as Shalva's minister, twenty-five/hundred arrows), quotes and sequence all match. Only the opening 'old enemy... against Dwaraka' framing relies on wider corpus context.

statements.claim: The passage opens with Krishna established in the highest duty of the householder, the one who keeps the home-fire.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.28: 'āsthitasya paraṃ dharmaṃ kṛṣṇasya gṛha-medhinām' — Krishna who had recourse to the supreme dharma of the householder (gṛhamedhin, keeper of the domestic fire).

statements.claim: Sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens made their home in Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered summary of BP 10.90.28-45: 'Krishna has sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens' (the 16,000-plus-one-hundred-plus figure of the earlier enumeration).

statements.claim: Eight of the queens are named in an earlier passage as the chief jewel-women, Rukmini at their head; the rest pass as a crowd.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.29: 'tāsāṃ strī-ratna-bhūtānām aṣṭau yāḥ prāg udāhṛtāḥ' — of them, eight previously declared as the jewel-women; Rukmini heads the chief queens in the earlier enumeration (corpus's Rukmini episodes; pack character list includes Rukmini).

statements.claim: On every one of these queens Krishna begot ten sons; the arithmetic runs past a hundred and sixty thousand.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.30: 'ekaikasyāṃ daśa daśa kṛṣṇo 'jījanad ātmajān' (ten and ten sons on each one); 16,100+ × 10 exceeds 160,000 (16,108 wives × 10 = 161,080).

statements.claim: Among the sons a few names rise to the surface: Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba, Diptiman, Bhanu, Pushkara, Vedabahu, Shrutadeva, Sunandana.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.32-33 names Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Dīptimān, Bhānu, Puṣkara, Vedabāhu, Śrutadeva and Sunandana; Sāmba is added by the pack's own summary ('among the foremost are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba and others') and is Krishna's son throughout the corpus.

statements.claim: No one born in this family was poor, and no one had few children; the men of the line of Yadu were famous for their deeds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.38-39: 'na hy etasmin kule jātā adhanā abahu-prajāḥ / yadu-vaṃśa-prasūtānāṃ puṃsāṃ vikhyāta-karmaṇām' — near-verbatim.

statements.claim: Where the old reckoning attempts a total it runs into the crores and beyond, and the book asks: who could count the Yadavas?
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.40-41: 'tisraḥ koṭyaḥ sahasrāṇām aṣṭāśīti-śatāni ca / saṅkhyānaṃ yādavānāṃ kaḥ kariṣyati mahātmanām' — a count in the crores, then 'who will count the great-souled Yadavas?'

statements.claim: Pradyumna married the daughter of Rukmi, and their son Aniruddha married Rukmi's granddaughter — the same house joined twice over.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.35-36: 'sa rukmiṇo duhitaram upayeme mahā-rathaḥ / sa cāpi rukmiṇaḥ pautrīṃ dauhitro jagṛhe tataḥ' — the great warrior [Pradyumna] wed Rukmi's daughter; the daughter's son [Aniruddha] took Rukmi's granddaughter.

statements.claim: From Aniruddha came Pratibahu, and from Pratibahu, Subahu — names trailing into a line too long to follow.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.37: 'pratibāhur abhūt tasmāt subāhus tasya cātmajaḥ' — from him came Pratibāhu; Subāhu was his son.

statements.claim: Vajra, the grandson of Pradyumna through Aniruddha, alone would survive the destruction by the mace — the last days of Dwaraka, when the Yadava houses turned their weapons upon one another.
statements.evidence: Pack's rendered summary: 'Pradyumna's grandson through Aniruddha is Vajra, who alone would survive the destruction by the mace'. Note textual variance: v.37's immediate line runs Aniruddha→Pratibahu→Subahu, while the tradition (and this pack's summary) makes Vajra Aniruddha's son and sole survivor; the story follows the pack summary, its intended reading.

statements.claim: The text explains the family's size: in the war between gods and demons terrible demon-lords had been slain, and to hold such forces in check the gods themselves took birth in the line of Yadu, with Hari as their measure and master.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.42-44: 'devāsurāhava-hatā daiteyā ye su-dāruṇāḥ / tan-nigrahāya hariṇā proktā devā yadoḥ kule / teṣāṃ pramāṇaṃ bhagavān prabhutvenābhavad dhariḥ' — the fierce Daiteyas slain in the gods' war were to be checked by gods born in Yadu's line; Hari was their authority.

statements.claim: The book turns from counting to the smallest record — how Krishna slept, sat, walked, spoke, played and bathed among his family.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.45: 'śayyāsanāṭanālāpa-krīḍā-snānādi-karmasu' — sleeping, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing and the like.

statements.claim: After millions upon millions, the truest measure of the man is an ordinary day in the middle of it all — a householder at the home-fire.
statements.evidence: Closing synthesis by the author, mirroring the passage's frame (v.28 householder dharma → v.45 daily acts); interpretive, not a sourced fact.

notes: Textually dense but every enumeration, name and genealogy matches BP 10.90.28-45 or the pack summary. Flagged variance: Vajra's slot in the genealogy (v.37 lists Pratibahu/Subahu as Aniruddha's line; the summary names Vajra as the surviving grandson) — story follows the pack summary as instructed.

statements.claim: Krishna chose the ground himself, walking the edge of the forest at sunrise after his morning ablutions with the elders of the Yadu house following.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'when the sun rose in the clear morning, Hrishikesha... having performed his morning ablution and sat for some time at the outskirt of the forest, began to survey it for finding out a site... The principal members of the Yudu race followed him.'

statements.claim: Krishna announces the site and its name: the city will be celebrated on earth as Dwaravati, like Indra's Amaravati; he is laying out courtyards, promenades, well-levelled roads and inner quarters, and bids the Yadavas take land, lay out gardens and crossings, survey roads and walls, and send for masons and artisans.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115 speech: 'I have also selected the name under which it will be celebrated on earth... this city of mine will be celebrated on earth by the name of Dwāravati like unto Indra's Amarāvti... I am laying out courtyards, promenades, well-levelled roads and inner appartments... Let all of you take lands for building houses; let gardens and crossings of four roads be laid out and let a survey of roads and walls be taken... masons be sent round the country.'

statements.claim: The Yadavas set about it that very day — some measuring plots with ropes, others honoring the tutelary deity with gifts to the brahmins — while the masons gather timber and stone and raise the gate and the boundary line.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: Yadavas 'engaged in measuring their own lands with ropes' and 'began to worship the tutelary deity by adorning the Brahmanas'; the masons 'collected all the materials for building the fort and began to lay out the gate and the boundary line.'

statements.claim: Krishna calls on Vishwakarma, the celestial architect, and he comes and stands before Krishna, saying: 'You are adorable to me as grandfather Brahma and as the three-eyed Shiva; there is no difference among the three. Command me as you command the three worlds.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Krishna thought of Viswakarmā... the celestial architect... came there and stood before Krishna'; his speech: 'thou art adorable unto me as the grand-father (Brahmā) and the three-eyed deity (Siva)... there is no difference amongst the three... do thou... issue command to me as thou dost order the three worlds.'

statements.claim: Krishna commands: 'Build me such a city that it may be celebrated on earth like Amaravati, so that mortals may see the beauty of this city and of the Yadu race.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Build for me such a city that it may be celebrated on earth like Amarāvati... so that the mortals may see the beauty of my city and of the Yadu race.'

statements.claim: Vishwakarma agrees on one condition: the city must be so vast that even the four oceans might range within it, so Krishna asks the ocean — the lord of rivers — to withdraw twelve yojanas.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'thy city will not sufficiently accommodate such a number of men. So very extensive should be thy city that even the four oceans, in their full forms, may range here'; Krishna to the ocean, 'lord of rivers': 'if you have any respect for me, then withdraw thy form in the water extending over twelve yojanas.'

statements.claim: Temples rise for Brahma, Indra and the gods of fire and water; four gates — Shudraksha, Aindra, Bhallata and Pushpadantaka — are set in the walls; the houses of the high-souled Yadavas go up street by street.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115: 'Temples... were built for Brahmā, the god of sacrifices, Indra, the presiding deities of fire and water and other gods. They then constructed the four gates... (namely Shudrāksha, Aindra, Bhallāta and Pushpadantāka)... the houses of the high-souled Yadavas were constructed.' (Dutt renders the four gates as gates 'of the temples'; the story sets them in the city walls — minor placement variance, same names.)

statements.claim: A few days after the founding, with Rishabha's consent, Balarama married Revati, the good-natured daughter of King Revata.
statements.evidence: HV 1.115 pack excerpt: 'A few days after with Reshava's consent Baladeva acquired the good-natured daughter of Revata, by name Revati.' Near-verbatim. (Variant in pack: VP 5.25 has Rāma sport two months in Vraja and marry Revatī, daughter of Raivata, on returning to Dwārakā; the story follows the HV reading, matching the pack's index summary.)

statements.claim: Balarama, Krishna's elder brother and the strong arm of the house, binds the Yadus by kinship to the line of Revata — the new city's first great household.
statements.evidence: Balarama's identity as Krishna's elder brother is corpus-wide fact, but the 'first great household' and kinship-significance of the match are the author's framing; HV gives the marriage only the single sentence the story itself quotes.

statements.claim: So Dwaraka began: the sea pushed back, the walls raised, and the elder brother married — a home complete only when someone begins a life inside it.
statements.evidence: Closing literary synthesis; rhetorical, not a sourced fact.

notes: Very close paraphrase of HV 1.115 (the city-founding speech, Vishwakarma exchange, ocean's twelve-yojana withdrawal, gates and the closing Revati sentence). Story follows the HV chronology (marriage a few days after the founding) rather than the VP variant (after two months in Vraja), which the pack itself flags.
